evidence.claim: A winding paved road through Rogue River canyons and forested slopes
evidence.quote: The entire route is a narrow, winding, paved road

evidence.claim: A winding paved road through Rogue River canyons and forested slopes
evidence.quote: Much of the drive provides a view of the deep river canyon with impressive rock walls bordered by forested slopes.

evidence.claim: The Galice-Hellgate Back Country Byway follows a narrow, winding paved road, with single-lane sections and occasional turnouts.
evidence.quote: The entire route is a narrow, winding, paved road and is suitable for passenger car travel. A portion of the byway is single lane with occasional turnouts.

evidence.claim: The Bureau of Land Management presents Rogue River country as its central attraction: canyon rock walls, forested slopes and places to reach the river.
evidence.quote: The beautiful Rogue River country is the focal point of the Galice-Hellgate Backcountry Byway.

evidence.claim: canyon rock walls, forested slopes and places to reach the river.
evidence.quote: Numerous river access points and developed recreation sites allow you to experience the river and its variety of recreation experiences. Much of the drive provides a view of the deep river canyon with impressive rock walls bordered by forested slopes.

evidence.claim: One stretch climbs away from the river into the Siskiyou Mountains, with views of mountains and Douglas fir.
evidence.quote: During one portion of this 39-mile route, the road climbs away from the river and into the Siskiyou Mountains, treating you to a spectacular view of nearby mountains and stands of Douglas fir.

evidence.claim: Allow one to two hours to visit the byway, with pullouts and developed recreation sites along the route.
evidence.quote: Time to Allow Allow 1-2 hours to visit the byway

evidence.claim: with pullouts and developed recreation sites along the route.
evidence.quote: Pullouts and recreation sites provide opportunities to view scenery and wildlife.

evidence.claim: Galice began as a mining community in 1852, first occupying Galice Creek rather than its present site on the Rogue.
evidence.quote: Galice was officially settled in 1852 as a mining community, deriving its name from one of its founders, Louis Galice.  It was at first called Galiceburg, and located on Galice Creek upstream from the Rogue River.  Today it sits on the Rogue, downstream from the junction with Galice Creek.

evidence.claim: Logging displaced mining in the mid-20th century, then gave way to tourism.
evidence.quote: Logging replaced mining as the town's principal industry in the mid 20th century, before giving way in turn to the tourist trade.

evidence.claim: The trail reached at Grave Creek has a separate history: the Takelma Indians developed it, and miners and settlers later improved it as they moved deeper into the canyon.
evidence.quote: This historic trail was originally developed by the Takelma Indians and improved by miners and settlers as they moved deeper into the canyon.

evidence.claim: At Rand, Civilian Conservation Corps workers built roads and trails and developed campgrounds in the surrounding national forest after a camp opened there in 1933.
evidence.quote: That same year, a Civilian Conservation Corps camp was established at Rand.  Known as Camp 1650, it was initially staffed by 18 enrollees.  While most of the Rand area projects were managed by the Forest Service, the Civilian Conservation Corps workers constructed buildings, built roads and trails, and developed campgrounds in the surrounding National Forest.

evidence.claim: after a camp opened there in 1933.
evidence.quote: The Civilian Conservation Corps was created in 1933.  That same year, a Civilian Conservation Corps camp was established at Rand.

evidence.claim: Begin at the Merlin exit from I-5 and travel west on Merlin-Galice Road through Merlin.
evidence.quote: The byway begins as you exit the freeway and travel the Merlin-Galice Road west. Four miles into the route you will travel through the town of Merlin.

evidence.claim: Continue through Galice to the former ranger station at Rand, now home to the Smullin Visitor Center.
evidence.quote: follow the Merlin-Galice Road 19 miles (31 km) west through the towns of Merlin and Galice.

evidence.claim: now home to the Smullin Visitor Center
evidence.quote: In 1996, the Bureau of Land Management's visitor center that occupies the old ranger station office was named the Smullin Visitor Center

evidence.claim: At Grave Creek, the byway provides access to the Rogue River National Recreation Trail.
evidence.quote: The byway provides access to the Rogue River National Recreation Trail at Grave Creek.

evidence.claim: Canyon rock walls rise beside forested slopes along much of the drive.
evidence.quote: Much of the drive provides a view of the deep river canyon with impressive rock walls bordered by forested slopes.

evidence.claim: Merlin began its railroad story under another name. The station established here in 1883 was called Jump Off Joe, after a local stream.
evidence.quote: A new railroad station in this location in 1883 was called "Jump Off Joe" for a local stream.

evidence.claim: In October 1886 it became Merlin, a name chosen by a railroad civil engineer for the falcons he saw here.
evidence.quote: The station was renamed "Merlin" in October 1886. The name came from a railroad civil engineer who named it for the merlins (a type of falcon) he saw in the area.

evidence.claim: The post office moved to the station vicinity and took the same name in 1891.
evidence.quote: then moved to the vicinity of the railroad station and renamed Merlin in 1891.

evidence.claim: The community sits in the Jumpoff Joe Creek valley, four miles east of its meeting with the Rogue, in an area known for fishing and whitewater rafting.
evidence.quote: It sits in the valley of Jumpoff Joe Creek, 4 miles (6 km) east of where that stream joins the Rogue River.

evidence.claim: in an area known for fishing and whitewater rafting
evidence.quote: The area is known for sport fishing and whitewater rafting on the Rogue River.

evidence.claim: On the byway, Merlin comes four miles after the I-5 exit.
evidence.quote: Four miles into the route you will travel through the town of Merlin.

evidence.claim: The original Galiceburg stood upstream on Galice Creek; Galice now occupies the Rogue River below the creek junction.
evidence.quote: It was at first called Galiceburg, and located on Galice Creek upstream from the Rogue River.  Today it sits on the Rogue, downstream from the junction with Galice Creek.

evidence.claim: The post office also moved downriver in 1922, before closing entirely in 1927.
evidence.quote: By 1922, however, the Post Office was moved down the river, and it closed entirely in 1927.

evidence.claim: Settled as a mining community in 1852, it took its name from founder Louis Galice.
evidence.quote: Galice was officially settled in 1852 as a mining community, deriving its name from one of its founders, Louis Galice.

evidence.claim: Gold prospecting made the creek busy in the 1850s, but mining did not remain the principal industry.
evidence.quote: The creek was a hot spot for gold prospecting in the 1850s.

evidence.claim: Logging took that role in the mid-20th century, followed by tourism. Nearby Hellgate Canyon became a filming location for parts of the 1975 John Wayne film Rooster Cogburn.
evidence.quote: Logging replaced mining as the town's principal industry in the mid 20th century, before giving way in turn to the tourist trade.  Hellgate Canyon, located nearby, was the site of filming for parts of John Wayne's 1975 film Rooster Cogburn.

evidence.claim: Before Rand had a ranger residence, Jesse P. Dewitt lived in a tent for eight years.
evidence.quote: Dewitt was forced to live in a tent for eight years, from 1909 until 1916.

evidence.claim: Jesse P. Dewitt
evidence.quote: Jesse P. Dewitt became the first district ranger.

evidence.claim: The mining company that owned the site finally agreed in 1916 to rent the Forest Service a parcel for one dollar a year.
evidence.quote: In 1916, the mining company finally agreed to rent a small parcel of land to the Forest Service for one dollar per year.

evidence.claim: The mining company that owned the site
evidence.quote: the Rand site (which was owned by a local mining company)

evidence.claim: Civilian Conservation Corps workers later built and improved the station structures.
evidence.quote: All the historic structures at the Rand Ranger Station were either built or improved by Civilian Conservation Corps workers under the supervision of Forest Service rangers.

evidence.claim: Their camp buildings are gone, but the Forest Service structures they built survive.
evidence.quote: While all of the buildings from Civilian Conservation Corps camp are now gone, the Forest Service structures built by Civilian Conservation Corps still exist and are in good condition.

evidence.claim: The Bureau of Land Management acquired the property from the Forest Service in 1970. In 1996, its visitor center received the Smullin name.
evidence.quote: In 1970, the Bureau of Land Management acquired the Rand property from the Forest Service.

evidence.claim: In 1996, its visitor center received the Smullin name.
evidence.quote: In 1996, the Bureau of Land Management's visitor center that occupies the old ranger station office was named the Smullin Visitor Center

evidence.claim: The former station office now serves as a visitor center.
evidence.quote: The Rand Ranger Station office is now a visitor center.

flags: BLM gives 40 miles; FHWA gives 39. Length omitted pending resolution. Rand mileage also differs: 18 miles in BLM, 19 in the station article.
Cache does not document road construction or designation date; overview uses corridor history without calling the trail the road.
Travel direction follows BLM from I-5 through Merlin and Galice to Rand and Grave Creek, reversing the strip-town mile ordering.
Current Merlin wording implied the engineer personally renamed the station in 1886; cache supports the name origin but not that act.
